title: Fire staffing plan, debt policy and grants overhaul
subtitle: Parking rates, 2024-2026 fees, Carnegie Library museum study, housing fund application, and two large development proposals heard.
overview: Council endorsed a phased fire staffing model, to be confirmed in the 2024-2026 budget, and released capital funding for a new fire rescue pumper truck. It also loosened its debt policy, allowing inter-reserve borrowing up to a set limit and removing the per-project debt cap, and replaced the community cash grants and neighbourhood matching fund with separate neighbourhood and sports and recreation grant policies. The arts grant policy was deferred.

Residents will see a 4% increase in monthly parking permit rates for 2024 and no change to hourly rates. Council also approved fees and charges for 2024-2026 across several departments, released funding for green building and facilities work, and directed staff to study moving the City of Waterloo Museum into the former Carnegie Library. Staff will prepare an application to the federal Housing Accelerator Fund.

Two informal public meetings were held on large proposals: converting an office building at 180 King Street South to residential, and a multi-tower development on King Street North and Weber Street North. No decisions were made. The mayor also said after the meeting that strong mayor powers are optional and she intends to delegate budget authority back to the CAO.

decisions.detail: Council approved releasing capital funding for a new fire rescue pumper from development charges and endorsed a phased staffing model subject to the 2024-2026 budget {{vote:m16}}.
Council removed the per-project debt limit, set a 20-year maximum debenture amortization, and allowed inter-reserve borrowing up to an internal limit {{vote:m4}}.

Council replaced the cash grants and matching fund policies with neighbourhood and sports and recreation grant policies, deferred the arts policy, and will dissolve the Community Grants Committee at the end of 2023 {{vote:m5}}.
Council approved a 4% monthly permit increase and no hourly rate increase for 2024, and allowed the Parking Reserve Fund to temporarily fall below its minimum threshold {{vote:m12}}.
Council directed staff to conduct a feasibility study on moving the City of Waterloo Museum to the former Carnegie Library {{vote:m13}}.
Council directed staff to prepare an application to the federal Housing Accelerator Fund for the initiatives in the staff report {{vote:m15}}.
Council released $526,000 from the Climate Action Reserve Fund for 2023 Green Building Policy implementation {{vote:m3}}.
Council approved the budget timeline, with the proposed budget to be released December 11, 2023, and revisions to policy FC-012 {{vote:m7}}.

debate: On carbon budgeting, a delegate said city emissions reductions fall well short of targets and urged carbon budgets alongside financial ones. One councillor questioned whether a community-wide carbon budget is feasible when a corporate one is already complex. Council noted a related line item in the budget strategy.

On the debt policy, councillors asked how climate projects that save energy costs would be treated and how 'strategic priority' would be defined. Staff said savings are not guaranteed and priorities are set through budget deliberations. Staff said internal borrowing avoids external costs and timing limits, and involves small sums relative to the capital budget.

On the fire plan, one councillor noted that endorsing the staffing model effectively commits the city to hiring ahead of the final master plan, while another supported acting now for resident safety. Staff said the final plan returns in fall 2023 and numbers could change then.

On grants, councillors asked about a gap for cultural events that do not fit the arts stream, the small size of the sports committee, and reporting back on results. Staff said they would help groups find other funding and could include a first-year update.

At the public meetings, a resident asked that the 180 King Street South building keep its height, wide sidewalks and trees, and raised traffic concerns. At the King Street North proposal, a resident asked how deeper foundations would protect groundwater flow through the moraine. Councillors asked about traffic, parking levels and a community meeting.
